units.name: Data and events that move markets

terms.short: Rate at which the RBI lends to banks
terms.definition: The rate at which the RBI lends to banks for short periods, against government bonds as collateral. It's the rate the Monetary Policy Committee votes on: raised to cool inflation, cut to support growth. Other short-term rates move around it.
examples: The RBI raised the repo rate by 25 bp in October 2026, to 5.50%.
The client asked why her home loan EMI went up: her bank's rate is linked to the repo rate.
Risk runs the bond book through a 50 bp jump in the repo rate every week.
terms.fill: To cool inflation, the MPC votes to raise the ____, and the rest of the RBI's corridor moves with it.
wrong: Rate banks pay on savings accounts
Rate the government pays on a 10-year bond
Rate at which banks lend to their best customers
terms.note: Repo is short for repurchase agreement: the bank sells bonds to the RBI and agrees to buy them back.

calcs.q: The repo rate is 5.50%. What is it after a 25 bp cut?

tf.s: When the RBI raises the repo rate by surprise, bond yields usually rise and bond prices fall.

terms.short: RBI panel that votes on the repo rate
terms.definition: The six-member committee that sets the repo rate: the RBI Governor, two other RBI officials and three outside members chosen by the government. It meets at least four times a year, usually six, and decides by majority vote, with the Governor breaking any tie.
examples: The MPC voted 6–0 to raise rates, though two members wanted to keep the stance neutral.
The bond desk cut duration the day before the MPC meeting.
The client asked who decides rates in India: the six-member MPC, three from the RBI and three from outside.
terms.fill: Six members, three from the RBI and three from outside, vote on the repo rate about every two months in the ____.
wrong: SEBI's board that approves F&O rules
Government panel that writes the Budget
Committee of bank chiefs that sets loan rates

tf.s: The RBI Governor can overrule the rest of the MPC whenever they disagree.
tf.why: Decisions go by majority. The Governor's casting vote only counts in a tie.

terms.short: RBI's signal of which way rates lean next
terms.definition: The short phrase the RBI's rate-setters attach to each decision to say which way they lean next, such as accommodative, neutral or tightening. Markets read a change of wording as closely as the rate move itself.
examples: The hike was expected; the switch in stance to calibrated tightening is what sank bonds.
The economist says the policy stance matters more than the hike, because it tells you what comes next.
Risk asked the bond desk how it would position if the RBI changed its policy stance to neutral.
terms.fill: The MPC kept rates on hold but changed its ____ from neutral to accommodative, hinting at cuts ahead.
wrong: The vote count at an MPC meeting
The RBI's forecast for GDP growth
The rate banks charge their best borrowers

tf.s: A neutral stance means the MPC has promised not to change rates.
tf.why: It means the next move could go either way, depending on the data.

terms.short: Leaning towards higher rates to fight inflation
terms.definition: Leaning towards tighter policy: higher rates, or keeping them high for longer, to bring inflation down. A hawk on the MPC worries more about inflation than about growth.
examples: The minutes were hawkish: three members flagged food prices.
The bond desk sold 10-year bonds after the governor sounded hawkish in the press conference.
The client asked why her debt fund fell: the RBI sounded hawkish and bond yields rose.
terms.fill: The governor warned that inflation risks were rising and rate cuts were off the table. Bond traders called the tone ____.
wrong: Leaning towards lower rates to support growth
Unwilling to say anything about future rates
Selling bonds ahead of an auction

tf.s: A hawkish surprise from the RBI usually pushes bond yields up.

terms.short: Leaning towards lower rates to support growth
terms.definition: Leaning towards easier policy: lower rates, or keeping them low for longer, to support growth and jobs. A dove on the MPC worries more about growth than about inflation.
examples: A dovish policy sent bank stocks up and the 10-year yield down 10 bp.
The economist expects a dovish tone now that inflation is back near 4%.
The client asked why her bank stocks jumped: the RBI turned dovish, so markets expect rate cuts.
terms.fill: The MPC hinted at more cuts to help slowing growth, a ____ message that sent bond prices higher.
wrong: Leaning towards higher rates to fight inflation
Keeping the policy rate fixed for a year
Buying dollars to weaken the rupee

terms.short: The RBI's 4% CPI goal, with a 2% to 6% band
terms.definition: The goal the government sets for the RBI: consumer price inflation of 4%, with a band of 2% to 6%. If inflation stays outside the band for three quarters in a row, the RBI must write to the government explaining why and what it will do.
examples: With inflation at 6.5%, the RBI is above the top of its band.
The economist notes prices have run above the RBI's inflation target for six straight months.
The client asked why the RBI cares about 4%: that's the midpoint of its inflation target.
terms.fill: The government has told the RBI to aim for 4% CPI inflation, with room between 2% and 6%. That goal is the ____.
wrong: Highest inflation the government allows in the Budget
Inflation rate used to set bank deposit rates
Price rise that triggers a fuel tax cut
terms.note: The government kept the 4% target and the 2% to 6% band for April 2026 to March 2031.

terms.short: Yearly rise in the prices shoppers pay
terms.definition: How much the consumer price index, a basket of food, fuel, housing, clothing and services, has risen over the past year. It's the inflation measure the RBI targets, so the monthly release can move bond yields and rate bets.
examples: CPI came in at 5.4% against 5.1% expected, and the 10-year yield jumped 6 bp.
The bond desk stays light before every CPI inflation print.
The client asked why her FD barely grows in real terms: CPI inflation is eating most of the interest.
terms.fill: Each month the government reports how much the prices of food, fuel and household goods have risen over the past year. That figure is ____.
wrong: Rise in the prices factories pay for raw materials
Growth in the economy's total output
Rise in share prices over the year

terms.short: How a repo change reaches loan and deposit rates
terms.definition: How far, and how fast, a change in the repo rate passes through to the rates banks charge on loans and pay on deposits. Loans tied to the repo rate pass a change on quickly; fixed deposits and older loans take longer.
examples: The RBI cut 100 bp, but transmission to deposit rates has been slow.
The banking analyst says slow transmission to loan rates will protect bank margins this year.
The client asked why her loan rate didn't fall after the cut; transmission takes months.
terms.fill: The RBI cut rates by 50 bp, but banks lowered their lending rates by only 20 bp. Economists said the ____ was weak.
wrong: How the RBI broadcasts its policy decision
Moving money between bank accounts
The spread of a sell-off from one market to another

terms.said: U S D I N R, or dollar-rupee
terms.short: Rupees needed to buy one US dollar
terms.definition: The exchange rate between the US dollar and the rupee, quoted as how many rupees one dollar buys. When the number goes up, the rupee has weakened.
examples: USDINR jumped 30 paise as FPIs sold heavily.
Risk stresses the importers in the book for a 3% jump in USDINR.
The client asked what USDINR at 88 means: it takes ₹88 to buy one US dollar.
terms.fill: If one dollar costs ₹88.50, the ____ rate is 88.50.
wrong: Dollars needed to buy one rupee
Value of the dollar against six major currencies
Interest rate gap between India and the US

calcs.q: USDINR moves from 85.00 to 87.55. By what percentage has it risen?

terms.short: Rupee losing value against other currencies
terms.definition: A fall in the rupee's value against other currencies, so each dollar costs more rupees. It makes imports like oil dearer and exports cheaper abroad, and cuts the dollar returns of foreign investors.
examples: IT stocks rallied on rupee depreciation, since they earn in dollars.
The pharma analyst counts rupee depreciation as a tailwind, since most sales are in dollars.
The client asked why her US fund beat the S&P 500: rupee depreciation added to her return.
terms.fill: The dollar went from ₹85 to ₹88 in six months, making imported oil dearer. That's ____.
wrong: The rupee gaining value against the dollar
The RBI printing more rupees
A cut in India's interest rates

tf.s: A weaker rupee usually helps Indian IT exporters.
tf.why: They earn in dollars and pay most of their costs in rupees.

terms.short: RBI dealing in dollars to steady the rupee
terms.definition: The central bank buying or selling dollars in the currency market to calm sharp moves in the rupee. It sells dollars from its reserves when the rupee is falling fast and buys them when inflows pile up. The RBI says it targets volatility, not a level.
examples: State-run banks were selling dollars at the highs, a sign of RBI intervention.
The FX desk thinks RBI intervention will cap the rupee's fall near the old low.
Risk asked how long RBI intervention can hold the rupee if foreign selling continues.
terms.fill: The rupee was sliding fast until state-run banks started selling dollars for the central bank. Traders called it ____.
wrong: The RBI changing the repo rate between meetings
The government taxing foreign investors
SEBI halting trading in currency futures

tf.s: When the RBI sells dollars to support the rupee, it also drains rupee cash from banks.
tf.why: Banks pay for the dollars in rupees, so system liquidity tightens.

terms.short: RBI's stock of foreign currency and gold
terms.definition: The foreign currency, gold and other foreign assets the RBI holds, mostly in US dollar bonds. They're the war chest it uses to defend the rupee, and it publishes the total every Friday.
examples: Reserves fell $5 billion in a week as the RBI defended the rupee.
The economist checks how many months of imports the forex reserves would cover.
The client asked why falling forex reserves were in the news: the RBI had sold dollars to defend the rupee.
terms.fill: The RBI's pile of dollars, other currencies and gold, which it draws on to defend the rupee, is its ____.
wrong: Dollars that Indian companies keep abroad
Cash that banks must keep with the RBI
The government's balance in its RBI account

terms.short: Exchange-traded futures on exchange rates
terms.definition: Futures on an exchange rate, traded on NSE and BSE. A USDINR contract is for $1,000, priced in rupees with a tick of ₹0.0025, and settles in cash against the official reference rate. Importers and exporters use them to hedge.
examples: We sold USDINR futures to hedge the export bills due in March.
The importer's treasury buys currency futures each month to fix the rupee cost of its bills.
The client asked if she can hedge her son's US tuition fees with currency futures on NSE.
terms.fill: An importer locks in the rupee cost of next month's dollar payment by buying $1,000 lots on NSE. They're trading ____.
wrong: Bank deposits held in foreign currency
Shares of Indian companies listed abroad
Options on the dollar index
terms.note: Each tick of ₹0.0025 on one $1,000 lot is worth ₹2.50. Monthly contracts stop trading two working days before the month's last business day.

calcs.q: One USDINR futures lot is $1,000, and the price rises from 88.0000 to 88.2500. What's the profit on one long lot?

terms.short: Forward rate above spot, from the rate gap
terms.definition: How much more a dollar for future delivery costs than one today. Rupee interest rates are higher than dollar rates, so the forward trades above spot by roughly the rate gap; it's usually quoted as an annual percentage.
examples: The one-year forward premium is close to the gap between Indian and US interest rates.
The exporter's treasurer sells dollars forward because the forward premium adds about 2% a year.
Risk notes the forward premium shrank as the gap between Indian and US rates narrowed.
terms.fill: Spot is 88.00 and the 12-month forward is 89.76, a 2% annual ____ that mirrors the gap in interest rates.
wrong: Extra a bank charges for exchanging cash
Price paid to buy a currency option
Gap between buying and selling rates at a money changer

calcs.q: Spot USDINR is 88.00, Indian rates are 6% and US rates 4%. Roughly where should the one-year forward trade?

tf.s: If Indian rates rise while US rates stay put, the USDINR forward premium tends to widen.

terms.short: Offshore rupee forward settled in dollars
terms.definition: A non-deliverable forward: a forward on the rupee traded outside India, mainly in Singapore, Dubai and London, and settled in dollars rather than rupees. Overnight moves there often show where the rupee will open at home.
examples: The rupee is seen opening weaker; NDFs are pointing to a 20-paise fall.
The FX dealer checks the overnight NDF moves before the onshore market opens.
Risk asked why the rupee gapped down at the open: offshore NDF trading had already priced the news.
terms.fill: Overnight, a rupee forward traded in Singapore and settled in dollars pointed to a weak open. That contract is an ____.
wrong: A forward the RBI uses to buy dollars from banks
A rupee bond sold to foreign investors
A forward that can't be cancelled before maturity

terms.short: Dollar's value against six major currencies
terms.definition: A measure of the US dollar against six major currencies, with the euro making up more than half. A rising index means a broadly stronger dollar, which usually weighs on the rupee and other emerging-market currencies.
examples: The dollar index is up 1% on the week, so the rupee's slip is no surprise.
The strategist says a weaker dollar index usually helps FPI flows into India.
The client asked why the rupee fell though India's news was good: the dollar index jumped worldwide.
terms.fill: A single number tracking the US dollar against the euro, yen, pound and three other currencies is the ____.
wrong: Index of US stocks priced in dollars
Rupees needed to buy one dollar
Rate the US central bank sets

tf.s: The rupee is one of the currencies in the dollar index.
tf.why: It's made of the euro, yen, pound, Canadian dollar, Swedish krona and Swiss franc.

terms.short: Borrow a low-rate currency, buy a high-rate one
terms.definition: Borrowing in a currency with low interest rates and investing in one with higher rates, such as the rupee, to earn the gap. It pays while exchange rates stay calm, and can unwind fast when they don't.
examples: Foreign funds piled into rupee bonds as a carry trade, then ran when the rupee fell 3% in a week.
Risk worries the carry trade into rupee bonds will unwind fast if the rupee slips.
The client asked what a carry trade is: borrow cheap in one currency, invest at a higher rate in another.
terms.fill: A fund borrows yen at 1%, buys rupee bonds yielding 7% and pockets the gap, as long as the rupee holds. That's a ____.
wrong: Buying a stock and holding it for years
Rolling futures from one month to the next
Shipping goods abroad on credit

terms.short: Country paying abroad more than it earns
terms.definition: When a country pays the rest of the world more for imports, interest and dividends than it earns from exports and money sent home. India usually runs one, mainly because of oil and gold imports, so it relies on foreign investment to fund it.
examples: A wider current account deficit leaves the rupee more exposed when FPIs pull money out.
The economist expects the current account deficit to narrow as oil prices fall.
The client asked why oil prices matter for the rupee: costly oil widens the current account deficit.
terms.fill: India's oil and gold imports cost more than it earns from exports and money sent home, so it runs a ____.
wrong: The government spending more than it collects in taxes
A bank's shortfall in its current accounts
The gap between India's imports and exports of goods only

terms.short: Where banks park spare cash with the RBI
terms.definition: The standing deposit facility: banks can leave surplus cash with the RBI overnight, and the RBI doesn't have to hand over bonds as collateral. Its rate, 25 bp below the repo rate, is the floor of the RBI's rate corridor.
examples: Banks are parking record sums in the SDF, so liquidity is in big surplus.
The bank's treasury desk parks its spare cash in the SDF overnight.
The economist notes the SDF rate now sets the floor for overnight rates.
terms.fill: Surplus cash that banks leave with the RBI overnight earns the ____ rate, the floor of the corridor.
wrong: Rate at which banks borrow overnight from the RBI in a pinch
Share of deposits banks must keep with the RBI
Rate banks pay on savings accounts

calcs.q: The repo rate is 5.50%. Where does the SDF rate sit?
calcs.why: The SDF is 25 bp below repo: 5.50% − 0.25% = 5.25%.

terms.short: Banks' emergency overnight loans from the RBI
terms.definition: The marginal standing facility: banks can borrow overnight from the RBI at a penalty rate, 25 bp above the repo rate, pledging government bonds, even ones they hold to meet their statutory liquidity rule. It's the ceiling of the corridor, and the Bank Rate is set equal to it.
examples: Liquidity is tight and banks are dipping into the MSF.
Risk tracks how often our bank borrows from the MSF, because it's the costliest window.
The economist says heavy MSF borrowing is a sign the system is short of cash.
terms.fill: Short of cash late in the day, a bank borrows overnight from the RBI at 25 bp above repo through the ____.
wrong: Account where banks park spare cash with the RBI
Short loan the RBI gives the government
Minimum balance a bank must keep with the RBI

calcs.q: The repo rate is 5.50%. What's the MSF rate?
calcs.why: The MSF is 25 bp above repo: 5.50% + 0.25% = 5.75%.

terms.short: Overnight rate banks pay each other
terms.definition: The rate at which banks lend to each other overnight without collateral, in the call money market. The weighted average of these deals is the RBI's operating target: it runs its liquidity operations to keep that rate close to the repo rate.
examples: The call rate drifted to 5.30%, near the floor, so there's too much cash around.
The money market desk watches the call rate all morning to price its overnight lending.
The economist says the call rate is trading above the repo rate, a sign liquidity is tight.
terms.fill: The RBI steers liquidity so that the rate banks charge each other for unsecured overnight loans stays near repo. That rate, its operating target, is the ____.
wrong: Price of a call option
Rate the RBI charges for emergency loans
Interest paid on a broker's margin funding

tf.s: When banks are flush with cash, the call rate tends to sink towards the SDF rate.
tf.why: Lenders have plenty to lend, so the overnight rate falls towards the floor of the corridor.

terms.short: Spare cash across the whole banking system
terms.definition: How much spare cash banks have in total, after meeting their reserve needs. In surplus, banks park the extra with the RBI and short-term rates sink; in deficit, they borrow from it and rates rise. Tax dates, government spending and RBI dollar sales all shift it.
examples: Advance tax outflows swung system liquidity into deficit this week.
The bond desk expects yields to ease as system liquidity swings into surplus.
Risk asked how tight system liquidity would affect our short-term borrowing costs.
terms.fill: In mid-June companies pay advance tax, cash drains from banks into the government's account, and overnight rates jump. Traders say ____ has tightened.
wrong: How easily one stock can be traded
Cash a fund keeps for redemptions
Total cash a company holds

terms.short: RBI auction that soaks up spare bank cash
terms.definition: A variable rate reverse repo: an auction in which banks bid to park surplus cash with the RBI for a set term, usually 7 days, at rates set by the bids. The RBI uses it to drain extra liquidity; its mirror image, the variable rate repo, lends cash in.
examples: The RBI ran a 7-day VRRR to soak up the cash from government spending.
The money market desk lends its spare cash to the RBI in the 7-day VRRR, earning a bit more than the SDF.
The economist says the RBI's VRRR auctions, where banks lend it cash at a variable rate, are back in heavy use.
terms.fill: With banks flush with cash, the RBI holds a 7-day auction to absorb the surplus. It's a ____.
wrong: Auction of new government bonds
Penalty rate for banks that fall short on reserves
Weekly sale of government bills

terms.short: RBI buying or selling government bonds
terms.definition: When the RBI buys or sells government bonds in the market to change how much cash banks have for months, not days. Buying bonds pumps cash in and tends to push yields down; selling drains cash.
examples: The RBI announced bond purchases through OMOs, and yields fell 8 bp.
The bond desk bought ahead of the OMO purchase, expecting yields to fall.
The client asked why bond prices rose; the RBI was buying bonds through OMO purchases.
terms.fill: To add cash to the banking system for the long haul, the RBI buys government bonds from banks in an ____.
wrong: Auction where the government sells new bonds
Market where banks lend to each other overnight
Rule on how much cash banks keep with the RBI

tf.s: When the RBI buys bonds in the market, it adds cash to the banking system.
tf.why: It pays for the bonds with new money that lands in banks' accounts.

terms.short: Share of deposits kept as cash with the RBI
terms.definition: The cash reserve ratio: the share of a bank's deposits it must keep as cash with the RBI, earning no interest. It's 3%, and cutting it frees money for banks to lend.
examples: The 100 bp cut in CRR in 2025 freed about ₹2.5 lakh crore for banks to lend.
The banking analyst says the CRR cut lets banks lend more of each deposit.
The client asked why banks keep some deposits idle at the RBI: that's the CRR, and it earns nothing.
terms.fill: A bank must keep 3% of its deposits as cash with the RBI, earning nothing. That 3% is the ____.
wrong: Share of deposits banks must invest in government bonds
Rate the RBI pays on banks' spare cash
Minimum capital a bank needs for its loans

calcs.q: A bank has ₹10,000 crore of deposits and the CRR is 3%. How much must it keep with the RBI?

terms.short: Share of deposits held in safe assets
terms.definition: The statutory liquidity ratio: the share of deposits a bank must hold in safe, liquid assets, mostly government bonds, plus cash and gold. It's 18%, which makes banks the biggest buyers of government debt.
examples: Banks hold well above their SLR, so they can pledge the extra bonds for repo.
The economist says banks' SLR holdings make them the biggest buyers of government bonds.
Risk counts only bonds above the SLR as free to pledge for funding.
terms.fill: Indian banks must keep 18% of their deposits in government bonds and other safe assets. That rule is the ____.
wrong: Share of deposits banks must keep as cash with the RBI
Cap on loans a bank can make to one company
Ratio of a bank's capital to its loans

terms.short: Bond issued by the government of India
terms.definition: A bond issued by the central government and sold through RBI auctions. It pays a coupon every six months and can run for 30 years or more. Strictly, treasury bills are government securities too, but on desks the name means these dated bonds.
examples: The 10-year G-sec yield rose 8 bp after the hawkish policy.
The bond desk is long the 10-year G-sec into the policy.
The client asked if her G-sec fund can lose money: yes, when yields rise, prices fall.
terms.fill: The 10-year bond the central government sells at RBI auctions, the benchmark for every Indian rates desk, is a ____.
wrong: A share in a government-owned company
A fixed deposit with a public sector bank
A loan the RBI gives to banks

tf.s: Individuals in India can buy G-secs straight from RBI auctions.
tf.why: Through the RBI Retail Direct portal, opened to individuals in 2021.

terms.short: Short government paper sold at a discount
terms.definition: Short-term borrowing by the central government that lasts 91, 182 or 364 days. It pays no coupon: it's sold below face value at a weekly RBI auction and repaid at face value, and the gap is the holder's return.
examples: The 91-day T-bill cut-off came in a touch above the repo rate.
The fund parks idle cash in the 91-day T-bill until it finds stocks to buy.
The client asked how her T-bill pays interest: she buys below ₹100 and gets ₹100 at maturity.
terms.fill: The government's 91-day paper, auctioned by the RBI every week below face value, is a ____.
wrong: A bill of exchange between two companies
A bond that pays a coupon every quarter
A note the RBI issues to banks overnight

calcs.q: A 364-day T-bill is sold at ₹94 and repays ₹100. Roughly what does it yield?
calcs.why: (100 − 94) ÷ 94 ≈ 6.4% for the year. The ₹6 is earned on the ₹94 you paid, not on ₹100.

terms.short: Bond issued by a state government
terms.definition: A bond issued by one of India's state governments and auctioned by the RBI on their behalf, usually every week. It yields a little more than a central government bond of the same length.
examples: SDLs are trading about 40 bp over G-secs, so the state bond fund looks attractive.
The bond desk likes SDL paper for the extra yield over central government bonds.
Risk treats each state's SDL as near-sovereign but still caps how much we hold.
terms.fill: A 10-year bond sold by the Maharashtra government to fund its budget is an ____.
wrong: A loan the RBI gives a state-owned bank
A bond issued by a city corporation
A grant from the centre to a state

terms.short: Average overnight interbank call rate
terms.definition: The weighted average call rate: the average rate at which banks lend to each other overnight in the uncollateralised call money market, weighted by volume. It is the RBI's operating target, so the RBI uses its liquidity tools to keep it close to the repo rate.
examples: WACR has drifted above the repo rate, so liquidity is tight.
The RBI's job is to keep WACR near the policy repo rate.
WACR fell towards the SDF rate as surplus liquidity piled up.
terms.fill: The RBI targets the ____, the volume-weighted overnight rate banks charge each other.
wrong: The rate the RBI pays on reverse repo
The 10-year government bond yield
The average rate on bank fixed deposits

reads.up: WACR rising above repo signals tight liquidity; short-term rates and bank funding costs climb.
reads.down: WACR slipping below repo signals surplus liquidity, often a sign the RBI is easing in practice.

terms.short: India's overnight interbank benchmark rate
terms.definition: The Mumbai Interbank Outright Rate, published daily by FBIL from call money trades in the first hour of the session. Overnight MIBOR is the floating leg of most Indian interest rate swaps, so it links the money market to the swap market.
examples: The swap pays fixed against overnight MIBOR.
MIBOR jumped when advance tax payments drained liquidity.
Corporate loans are sometimes priced as MIBOR plus a spread.
terms.fill: The floating leg of most Indian interest-rate swaps is the overnight ____.
wrong: The RBI's policy repo rate
The yield on a 91-day T-bill
The rate at which the RBI lends against bonds overnight

terms.short: Tri-party repo: collateralised overnight lending
terms.definition: Tri-party repo dealing and settlement, run by CCIL: overnight lending against government securities, with CCIL as the central counterparty. It is the biggest overnight money market in India, used by banks, mutual funds and others to park or borrow cash.
examples: Liquid funds park spare cash in TREPS overnight.
TREPS rates spiked at quarter-end as banks hoarded cash.
Because it is collateralised, TREPS usually trades a little below the call rate.
terms.fill: Mutual funds lend cash overnight against G-secs through CCIL in ____.
wrong: A bond issued by three banks together
A deposit scheme run by the RBI
A swap of fixed for floating rates

terms.short: Swap fixed against compounded overnight rate
terms.definition: A swap where one side pays a fixed rate and the other pays the overnight rate (MIBOR in India), compounded over the period. OIS rates show where the market expects the RBI's policy rate to go, and they are the main tool banks and funds use to bet on or hedge rate moves.
examples: The one-year OIS fell 15 bps after the dovish policy, pricing in a cut.
Pay fixed in OIS to hedge against the RBI hiking.
Foreign banks trade the OIS heavily ahead of the policy meeting.
terms.fill: The market's view of future RBI rates shows up most clearly in the one-year ____.
wrong: A bond whose coupon resets every night
An overnight loan from the RBI
A swap of rupees for dollars

reads.up: Rising OIS rates mean the market expects higher policy rates: bond yields and bank stocks often move with it.
reads.down: Falling OIS rates price in cuts; rate-sensitive sectors like banks, NBFCs and real estate tend to rally.

terms.short: A bank's tradeable short-term deposit
terms.definition: A short-term money market instrument issued by a bank, sold at a discount and repaid at face value, usually for up to a year. Banks issue more when deposits lag loan growth, so rising CD rates and volumes are a sign of a funding squeeze.
examples: Banks raised ₹50,000 crore through certificates of deposit as deposit growth lagged loans.
Three-month CD rates are 50 bps above the repo rate: funding is tight.
Liquid funds hold bank CDs alongside T-bills.
terms.fill: A bank borrowing for six months by selling a discounted, tradeable deposit issues a ____.
wrong: A fixed deposit held by a retail customer
A bond issued by the RBI
A loan from the RBI's discount window

reads.up: Rising CD rates and issuance signal banks struggling to fund loans with deposits: pressure on bank margins.
reads.down: Falling CD rates mean easy liquidity and comfortable funding for banks.

terms.short: The band between the RBI's SDF and MSF rates
terms.definition: The liquidity adjustment facility corridor: the range between the standing deposit facility rate (the floor, where banks park surplus cash) and the marginal standing facility rate (the ceiling, where they borrow in an emergency), with the repo rate in the middle. Overnight rates should stay inside it.
examples: Call rates hit the top of the LAF corridor at MSF during the tax outflow.
With surplus liquidity, WACR sank to the bottom of the LAF corridor.
The RBI keeps the LAF corridor narrow so overnight rates track repo.
terms.fill: Overnight rates are meant to stay between the SDF rate and the MSF rate, a band called the ____.
wrong: The range in which the rupee may move
The band for daily price limits on bonds
The gap between lending and deposit rates at banks

terms.short: Very short government borrowing for cash gaps
terms.definition: A short-term government security, for less than 91 days, issued to cover temporary mismatches between spending and tax receipts. It works like a T-bill but with a shorter, irregular tenor.
examples: The government issued a cash management bill before the advance tax inflow.
Cash management bills drained liquidity for a few weeks.
A 35-day cash management bill priced close to the T-bill curve.
terms.fill: A government security of under 91 days to cover a short gap before tax receipts arrive is a ____.
wrong: A bill the RBI issues to absorb dollars
A short-term loan to state governments
A company's short-term note

terms.short: 10-year yield minus 2-year yield
terms.definition: The difference between the 10-year and 2-year government bond yields, the standard measure of how steep the yield curve is. It widens (steepens) when markets expect growth or inflation later, and narrows or turns negative (inverts) when they expect rate cuts and slowdown.
examples: The 2s10s spread steepened 20 bps after the inflation surprise.
A negative 2s10s spread in the US has often come before a recession.
We put on a 2s10s steepener into the budget.
terms.fill: The 10-year yield at 7.0% and the 2-year at 6.6% gives a 40 bps ____.
wrong: The gap between the repo rate and the 10-year yield
The spread between corporate and government bonds
The difference between two dates in a swap

reads.up: A steeper 2s10s often means stronger growth or inflation expected ahead; it helps banks, which borrow short and lend long.
reads.down: A flatter or inverted 2s10s signals expected rate cuts or a slowdown; it often worries equity markets.

terms.short: Bet on the middle of the curve vs the ends
terms.definition: A three-leg yield-curve trade: buy (or sell) a middle maturity, like the 5-year, against the opposite position in a short and a long maturity, like the 2- and 10-year, sized so it doesn't care about parallel moves or the slope. It is a bet on curvature: whether the belly cheapens or richens.
examples: The 2-5-10 curve butterfly says the 5-year is cheap.
Sizing the curve butterfly by PV01 makes it neutral to parallel shifts.
Heavy supply in the 5-year sector made the curve butterfly pay off.
terms.fill: Buying the 5-year and selling the 2- and 10-year, neutral to level and slope, is a ____.
wrong: An option strategy with three strikes
A bet that all yields rise together
Switching from one bond to a newer issue

terms.short: Swap rate minus government bond yield
terms.definition: The difference between an interest rate swap rate (in India, the OIS) and the government bond yield of the same maturity. It moves with bank liquidity, bond supply and foreign flows. Traders bet on it widening or narrowing without taking a view on rates.
examples: The five-year swap spread turned negative as banks bought bonds hand over fist.
Heavy government borrowing pushed bond yields above OIS, moving the swap spread.
Foreign banks trade the swap spread rather than outright duration.
terms.fill: The 5-year OIS at 6.5% against a 5-year G-sec at 6.8% gives a −30 bps ____.
wrong: The gap between two corporate bond yields
The bid-ask spread on a swap
The difference between the repo and reverse repo rates

terms.short: Extra yield for lending long, not rolling short
terms.definition: The extra yield investors want for holding a long bond instead of rolling over short ones, beyond what they expect short rates to average. It rises with uncertainty about inflation and with heavy government borrowing, and pushes long yields up even if rate expectations don't change.
examples: Long yields rose on the borrowing announcement even though rate expectations didn't move: the term premium went up.
A rising term premium in US Treasuries spills over into Indian bonds.
The term premium explains why the curve stays steep with cuts priced in.
terms.fill: The extra yield for holding a 10-year bond over rolling 3-month bills, beyond expected rates, is the ____.
wrong: The premium paid on a new bond issue
The fee for extending a loan
The coupon on an inflation-linked bond

terms.short: G-secs foreigners can buy without limits
terms.definition: A route set up by the RBI in 2020 that lets non-residents buy specified government bonds with no investment limits. Bonds eligible under it are the ones global bond indices include, so FAR bonds see most foreign buying.
examples: Only FAR bonds made it into the global index.
Foreign funds bought ₹10,000 crore of Fully Accessible Route bonds in a week.
New 10-year issues are often designated under the Fully Accessible Route.
terms.fill: Specified G-secs that non-residents can buy without any limit fall under the ____.
wrong: The route for retail investors to buy G-secs
A channel for banks to borrow from the RBI
The trading platform for corporate bonds

terms.short: Indian bonds joining global benchmark indices
terms.definition: Global bond index providers adding Indian government bonds to their benchmarks, so funds that track them must buy. JP Morgan began adding Indian FAR bonds to its emerging-market index from June 2024, phased in over ten months. It brings steady foreign demand and supports the rupee.
examples: Bond index inclusion brought billions of dollars of passive buying into G-secs.
Yields fell as funds front-ran bond index inclusion.
Bond index inclusion makes Indian yields more sensitive to global flows.
terms.fill: Global funds having to buy Indian government bonds because they joined a benchmark is called ____.
wrong: A stock joining the Nifty 50
The RBI buying bonds in the market
A company listing its bonds on an exchange

reads.up: More index weight brings passive foreign buying: lower G-sec yields and support for the rupee.
reads.down: Outflows or a delay in inclusion remove that steady demand, so yields can rise and the rupee weaken.

terms.short: Nifty futures traded at GIFT City almost all day
terms.definition: Nifty 50 futures traded in dollars on NSE International Exchange at GIFT City, Gandhinagar, for nearly 21 hours a day. They replaced SGX Nifty in 2023. Because they trade before the Indian open, traders use them as the early read on where Nifty will open.
examples: GIFT Nifty is down 150 points, so expect a gap-down open.
US markets fell overnight and GIFT Nifty followed.
Check GIFT Nifty at 8 am before planning the day.
terms.fill: Traders check ____ before 9 am because it trades Nifty futures almost round the clock.
wrong: The pre-open auction on NSE
A Nifty ETF listed in Singapore
An index of stocks in Gujarat
terms.note: GIFT Nifty replaced SGX Nifty, which traded in Singapore, in July 2023.

reads.up: GIFT Nifty trading well above Nifty's last close points to a gap-up open.
reads.down: GIFT Nifty trading well below the close points to a gap-down open.

terms.short: The world's benchmark long-term rate
terms.definition: The yield on 10-year US Treasury bonds, the reference rate for global markets. When it rises, money tends to flow out of emerging markets like India, the dollar strengthens, and high-valuation stocks suffer. Indian bond yields and the rupee often move with it.
examples: The US 10-year yield jumped 20 bps and FPIs sold Indian equities.
A falling US 10-year yield helped the rupee recover.
IT stocks with US revenue care about the US 10-year yield through the dollar.
terms.fill: The yield on 10-year Treasuries, the ____, moves FPI flows into Indian markets.
wrong: India's 10-year government bond yield
The Federal Reserve's policy rate
The yield on a US corporate bond index

reads.up: A rising US 10-year usually means a stronger dollar and FPI outflows from India: pressure on the rupee and growth stocks.
reads.down: A falling US 10-year eases pressure on emerging markets, often bringing FPI inflows and a firmer rupee.

terms.short: How fast the economy's output is growing
terms.definition: The change in gross domestic product, the value of everything produced in the economy, usually quoted year on year for a quarter. India's official estimates come out about two months after each quarter ends. Real growth strips out inflation; nominal growth doesn't, and nominal growth is what company revenues and tax collections track.
examples: GDP growth came in at 7.8%, ahead of the 7.2% consensus, and banks led the rally.
Real GDP growth was strong, but with low inflation nominal growth was weak, and so were revenues.
Watch the GDP growth revision too: last quarter's number was cut.
terms.fill: The year-on-year rise in the value of everything the economy produced is ____.
wrong: The rise in prices paid by consumers
The growth of the stock market's value
The growth of the government's tax collections

reads.up: Faster growth than expected usually lifts cyclical stocks and banks; bond yields can rise if it makes rate cuts less likely.
reads.down: Slower growth than expected weighs on cyclicals and can raise hopes of rate cuts, which helps bonds.

terms.short: Government spending minus its income, borrowed
terms.definition: How much more the government spends than it earns from taxes and other income in a year, which it must borrow. It is quoted as a share of GDP and set as a target in each Union Budget. A bigger deficit means more government bonds to sell, which can push yields up.
examples: The Budget kept to its fiscal deficit target, and bond yields fell 8 basis points.
A wider fiscal deficit means a bigger borrowing calendar for G-secs.
Rating agencies watch the fiscal deficit and the debt it adds up to.
terms.fill: The gap between what the government spends and its income, which it fills by borrowing, is the ____.
wrong: The gap between the country's imports and exports
The fall in the rupee against the dollar
The shortfall in banks' cash reserves

reads.up: A wider fiscal deficit than planned means more bond supply and usually higher yields; rating agencies may grow cautious.
reads.down: A narrower deficit, or a credible path down, usually pulls bond yields lower and is read well by foreign investors.

tf.s: The fiscal deficit and the current account deficit are two names for the same gap.
tf.why: The fiscal deficit is the government's budget gap. The current account deficit is the country's gap in trade and income with the rest of the world.

terms.short: The government's yearly tax and spending plan
terms.definition: The central government's annual statement of spending, taxes and borrowing, presented by the Finance Minister in Parliament, usually on 1 February. In an election year an interim Budget comes in February and the full one after the new government forms, as in July 2024. For markets it sets the fiscal deficit target and borrowing, and it can change STT, capital gains tax and duties on whole sectors, so it is one of the year's biggest event days.
examples: The Union Budget raised STT on F&O, and broker stocks fell.
Option IVs climb into the Union Budget and crush the day after.
Infrastructure stocks rallied on the higher capex in the Union Budget.
terms.fill: The yearly statement, usually presented on 1 February, that sets taxes, spending and the borrowing plan is the ____.
wrong: The RBI's statement on interest rates
SEBI's yearly review of market rules
The government's report on the past year's economy

terms.short: Inflation without food and fuel
terms.definition: Consumer price inflation with food and fuel stripped out, because those swing with the monsoon and global oil prices. India's statistics office publishes headline CPI, and analysts work out core from it. The RBI watches core to judge how sticky price pressure is underneath.
examples: Headline CPI fell on cheaper vegetables, but core inflation stayed at 4%.
Sticky core inflation makes the RBI wary of cutting rates quickly.
Core inflation tells you about demand; food prices mostly tell you about the monsoon.
terms.fill: CPI inflation with food and fuel taken out is ____.
wrong: Inflation in wholesale prices
Inflation in food prices only
The RBI's target for inflation

tf.s: A fall in vegetable prices lowers core inflation.
tf.why: Core leaves food and fuel out, so vegetables move headline CPI, not core.

terms.short: Business survey: above 50 means expanding
terms.definition: Purchasing Managers' Index: a monthly survey of purchasing managers on orders, output, jobs and prices, compared with the month before. A reading above 50 means activity is expanding, below 50 contracting. India has separate manufacturing and services PMIs, out in the first days of each month, well before official data.
examples: Manufacturing PMI fell to 51 from 56: still growing, but much more slowly.
The services PMI's price index rose, a hint inflation may pick up.
PMIs come out early in the month, so traders use them ahead of the official numbers.
terms.fill: A monthly survey of purchasing managers where 50 separates growth from contraction is the ____.
wrong: The index of prices paid by consumers
An index of the 50 largest listed companies
The RBI's survey of household inflation expectations

tf.s: A PMI falling from 56 to 52 means activity shrank that month.
tf.why: Anything above 50 is still expansion. The fall means growth slowed, not that activity shrank.

terms.short: The US Fed's rate-setting committee
terms.definition: The Federal Open Market Committee: the US Federal Reserve body that sets the federal funds rate, meeting eight times a year. Its decisions and the chair's press conference move US yields and the dollar, which drive foreign flows into India, the rupee and the Nifty.
examples: A hawkish FOMC lifted the dollar, and the rupee hit a new low the next morning.
FPIs held back ahead of the FOMC decision.
The FOMC's dot plot showed fewer cuts than the market had priced in.
terms.fill: The US committee that meets eight times a year to set the federal funds rate is the ____.
wrong: India's monetary policy committee
The body that sets crude oil output
The US body that regulates stock exchanges

reads.up: A Fed that is more hawkish than expected (higher rates for longer) usually strengthens the dollar, lifts US yields and pulls foreign money out of India.
reads.down: A Fed that is more dovish than expected usually weakens the dollar and brings foreign flows back to Indian stocks and bonds.
